steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Conjunct melody moves by step (adjacent notes); disjunct melody leaps between distant notes — each creates different character.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Triadic melodies outline chord shapes; scalic melodies run up/down scales; arpeggio melodies break chords into individual notes.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Passing notes connect chord notes melodically; ornamental notes (acciaccatura, appoggiatura) decorate the main melody.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Ostinato is a repeated melodic pattern that provides a foundation — used extensively in Baroque, minimalism and popular music.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe how melody are used in a piece of music you have studied. Use musical vocabulary. | Compare how two different pieces use melody. Explain the effect in each case. | How could you use melody in your own composition or performance? Explain your choices.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: A detailed description using precise musical vocabulary (e.g. specific terms from the AQA elements list), referencing a named piece with accurate observations about how the elements are used and their | A comparison of two pieces identifying similarities and differences in how melody are used, explaining the different effects created in each musical context, using comparative language. | A practical application showing understanding of how melody can be manipulated in composition or performance, with specific examples of choices made and their intended effect.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always use PRECISE musical vocabulary — not vague descriptions like it sounds nice Reference SPECIFIC musical elements when analysing any piece For listening questions: identify elements FIRST, then explain their effect For study pieces: know the context, structure and key features in detail For performing: focus on accuracy, expression and interpretation For composing: show development of ideas, not just repetition
